title: Fine-Grained Iterative Adversarial Attacks with Limited Computation Budget
claim: Activation changes between successive attack iterations shrink sharply, and unevenly across layers, so most recomputation is redundant.
layout: 2 panels, left line plot and right heatmap, shared iteration axis
description: Two side-by-side empirical plots. The left panel is a line plot of relative change (y-axis) against attack iteration 1 to 10 (x-axis). A bold dashed red line with markers shows a normal model, and a bold dashed blue line shows a robust model. Faint translucent lines behind them show individual samples or layers. Both curves fall quickly and then flatten. The red curve starts near 0.22 and levels off around 0.06, and the blue curve stays near 0.01 or lower. The right panel is an annotated viridis heatmap titled 'Relative Error (×10^-2)'. Its rows are attack iterations T1 to T10 and its columns are layers L1 to L18. Numeric values appear in each cell. Error is highest, in yellow, at early iterations and deep layers such as L14 to L16. It is lowest, in dark purple, at late iterations. A colorbar sits on the right.
caption: Gradient-based Adversarial Attack
abstract: This work tackles a critical challenge in AI safety research under limited compute: given a fixed computation budget, how can one maximize the strength of iterative adversarial attacks? Coarsely reducing the number of attack iterations lowers cost but substantially weakens effectiveness. To fulfill the attainable attack efficacy within a constrained budget, we propose a fine-grained control mechanism that selectively recomputes layer activations across both iteration-wise and layer-wise levels. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently outperforms existing baselines at equal cost. Moreover, when integrated into adversarial training, it attains comparable performance with only 30% of the original budget.
